query: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) is an α + β dual-phase alloy with low hardness and poor friction and wear properties under extreme-service and high-contact-stress conditions. Earlier studies explored redesigning the bulk alloy, which risks compromising its original advantages, and several surface-modification approaches. Traditional thermal spraying and thermal plating produced weak coatings with poor substrate bonding; composite coatings suffered from uneven constituent dispersion and weak interfaces; and laser cladding could generate intermetallic compounds, high residual stresses, cracks, and crazing. Prior refractory high-entropy-alloy studies reported improved hardness and wear resistance, but the broader requirements of compositional homogeneity, strong bonding, mechanical stability, and preservation of TC4’s beneficial properties remain. Formulate one neutral, testable hypothesis for an intervention that could satisfy these requirements. Specify the intervention, proposed mechanism, predicted outcome relative to untreated TC4, operating or test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating via low-temperature cold-spray deposition to TC4 (Ti6Al4V) will enhance its surface hardness and wear resistance under high-contact stress conditions while preserving strong substrate bonding and avoiding significant intermetallic formation.
generation.material_initial_state: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) as an α + β dual-phase alloy exhibiting low hardness and poor wear performance under extreme-service conditions.
generation.intervention: Cold-spray deposition of a refractory HEA coating onto TC4.
generation.conditions: Performance is evaluated under extreme-service, high-contact stress and wear testing environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A homogeneous, nanostructured HEA coating that forms a graded interfacial microstructure ensuring robust metallurgical bonding with the TC4 substrate, without significant intermetallic phase development.
generation.mechanism: The low thermal input of cold-spray deposition minimizes alterations to the TC4 substrate and prevents the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds, while the inherent properties of the refractory HEA increase hardness and wear resistance at the surface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated TC4 samples will demonstrate a measurable increase in surface hardness and a reduced wear rate compared to untreated TC4, with maintained or improved bonding at the coating–substrate interface.
generation.baseline: The performance metrics (surface hardness, wear resistance, and bonding integrity) of untreated TC4 under similar extreme-service testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness is expected under high-contact stress regimes and may depend on achieving an optimal coating thickness and adhering to specific deposition parameters; deviations could lead to insufficient bonding or the onset of unwanted phase formations.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the optimal thickness and exact deposition parameters needed to maximize performance without triggering thermal-induced defects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of TC4 samples: one group with the cold-sprayed HEA coating and one uncoated control group. Subject both groups to standardized high-contact stress wear tests and conduct surface hardness measurements. Analyze the coating–substrate interface using SEM/TEM and assess phase composition with X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect any intermetallic formation.
measurements: Wear rate (mass or volume loss over a standardized number of cycles)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in surface hardness and a decreased wear rate relative to untreated TC4, or if notable intermetallic compounds or weak bonding at the interface are observed, the hypothesis is considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Applying a refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating via low-temperature cold-spray deposition to TC4 (Ti6Al4V) will increase surface hardness and improve wear resistance under extreme-service conditions, while preserving or enhancing the substrate bonding and avoiding detrimental intermetallic formation.
drafts.material_initial_state: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) as an α + β dual-phase alloy with low hardness and poor wear performance under high-contact stress conditions.
drafts.intervention: Cold-spray deposition of a refractory HEA coating onto TC4.
drafts.conditions: Tests conducted under extreme-service conditions simulating high-contact stress and wear environments.
drafts.structural_mediator: A homogeneous, nanostructured HEA coating that provides a graded microstructure at the interface to ensure strong metallurgical bonding without significant intermetallic phase formation.
drafts.mechanism: The low thermal input of cold-spray deposition minimizes changes to the TC4 substrate microstructure, preventing the formation of brittle intermetallics, while the inherent properties of the refractory HEA (high hardness and wear resistance) contribute to reducing surface damage.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Coated TC4 samples will exhibit a measurable increase in surface hardness and a reduced wear rate compared to untreated TC4, along with maintained or improved bonding strength at the coating–substrate interface.
drafts.baseline: Performance metrics (hardness, wear resistance, and substrate bonding) of untreated TC4 under similar testing conditions.
drafts.boundary: The improvement is expected in high-contact stress environments; however, effectiveness may depend on achieving an optimal coating thickness and deposition parameters. The hypothesis may not hold if the coating is too thin, insufficiently bonded, or if deviations in deposition parameters introduce unwanted thermal effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of TC4 samples; apply the cold-sprayed HEA coating to the test group while keeping a control group uncoated. Subject both groups to standardized high-contact stress wear tests and hardness measurements. Use microscopy (SEM/TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to evaluate the interface bonding, phase compositions, and any intermetallic formations.
measurements: Surface hardness (e.g., via Vickers or nanoindentation)
Wear rate (e.g., mass loss or volume loss over standardized cycles)
Phase composition (via XRD) to detect intermetallic compounds
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >20% increase in hardness and reduction in wear rate) compared to untreated TC4, or if significant intermetallic phases or poor bonding at the interface are observed, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
